new_statements.quote: Esan has at least two contrastive tones high (H) and low (L). Nouns exhibit inherent tonal specification, though verbs do not. Tone in Esan is not as lexically important as in other West African languages (i.e. Yoruba). Grammatically however, Esan maintains tonal patterns which distinguish declarative from interrogative sentences, affirmative from negative sentences, and past from present (non-past) tenses.
new_statements.citation: Rolle, Nicholas. 2010. On the syntactic distribution and morphological form of resumptive pronouns in Esan. M.A. forum paper, University of Toronto (Toronto Working Papers in Linguistics, MA Forum Papers).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Esan is described as a two-tone (H/L) language with lexical tone on nouns and grammatical tone on the clause; no opened source says anything about word stress or accent, either its position or its absence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the only accent-placement statement in the corpus (Thomas 1910 pp. 141-142, penultimate dynamic accent) is about Edo/Bini proper, not Esan.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone on nouns and sentence-level grammatical tone; description based on the Ogwa dialect (Esan West LGA) with other Esan dialects consulted; citation-form vs phrase-level stress not discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Rolle 2010 (the quoted source) describes the Ogwa dialect of Esan (Esan West LGA), with speakers of other Esan dialects consulted; Rolle notes 25-40 dialects. Thomas 1910's Ishan texts are from Irua. Glottolog esan1238 has no separate dialect codes that I could confirm. The only accent-placement statement encountered (Thomas 1910, 'Accent and tone', pp. 141-142: dynamic accent normally penultimate) is for Edo/Bini proper (bini1246) and must not be attributed to Esan.

sources.note: Section 2.4 'Overview of the phonology' (pp. 24-26, Ogwa dialect): consonant and vowel inventories, then p. 26: two contrastive tones H and L, nouns have inherent tone, verbs do not, grammatical tone marks sentence types and tense. The words stress/accent do not occur anywhere in the paper.

sources.citation: Thomas, Northcote W. 1910. Anthropological Report on the Edo-speaking Peoples of Nigeria, Part II: Linguistics. London: Harrison and Sons.
sources.note: The section 'Accent and tone' (pp. 141-142) belongs to the EDO (Bini) GRAMMAR: 'The dynamic accent falls normally on the penultimate, but in words ending in ia, ie, oa, ua, etc., it usually falls on the antepenultimate' and 'two tones, the high and the low'. This is about Edo proper (bini1246), not Ishan. The Ishan material is texts from Irua (pp. 74ff.) and comparative vocabulary; no Ishan accent statement. Transliteration key defines a stress mark 'Dynamic accent (stress)'.
